title: Behaviour-locked covariance carried 71% of reliable pair-specific coactivity in 40 moving C. elegans and 47-52% in 22 larval zebrafish; wiring explained under 8% of the remainder
abstract: Question: earlier campaign work found that pair-specific functional connectivity (FC) is highly reliable, but wiring explains only 5-24% of it after node and distance effects. What sets the large, reliable, non-wiring part? Approach: in each animal, a cross-validated ridge model predicted each neuron or region from measured behaviour (worm: velocity, reversal, head bending, pumping; zebrafish: swims and dark flashes). The correlation of z-scored traces then splits exactly into a behaviour-locked part, a residual part and a cross term. After node fixed effects and distance terms were removed, split halves of animals gave the share of the reliable pair-specific coactivity that each part carries, and the correlation of wiring with the noise-free pattern of each part (rho). Nulls: time-shifted behaviour, node-label permutation and a simulation with known truth; leave-one-animal-out jackknife intervals. Results: in 40 freely moving off-food worms (Atanas 2023; 107 neurons, 4,293 pairs), the behaviour-locked part carried 0.712 (0.688-0.736) of the reliable pair pattern (time-shifted null 0.027). Locomotion features alone carried 0.708. Rank-3 node factors of this part, fit on independent animals, removed 70% of the reliable pattern. Anatomy (gap junctions, chemical synapses, shared input and output, contact) explained 1.9% of the locked part (rho 0.138) and 5.1% of the residual part (rho 0.226); with class, transmitter, type and lineage added, 7.7% of the residual. In 8 on-food worms (Dag 2023) the locked share was 0.490 (0.372-0.608; null 0.092), with more weight on pumping. In 22 larval zebrafish (Legare 2025; 65 regions) the swim- and flash-locked part carried 0.466 (0.397-0.535; null 0.048), 0.520 in 16 swimmers; there, locked and residual patterns had the same shape (calibrated r 0.72) and anatomy related to both equally (rho 0.34, 0.39). In simulation the share estimate was conservative and rho was accurate. Limitations: a linear behaviour model cannot separate activity that drives behaviour from activity that follows it, and it misses unmeasured behaviour; connectomes and activity come from different animals; the on-food cohort is small; zebrafish data are region averages at 1 volume/s; no fly or mouse data; analyses chosen after earlier campaign results.
